newsitem.title: UK: Chance of renewed IRA truce are bleak - Sinn Fein.
newsitem.headline: Chance of renewed IRA truce are bleak - Sinn Fein.

text.p: The prospect of a renewed IRA ceasefire looked dim on Tuesday after a spokesman for its political wing, Sinn Fein, said the chances for a truce were "virtually non-existent".

Sinn Fein's chief negotiator Martin McGuinness blamed Prime Minister John Major for the bleak outlook because Britain had rejected proposals by Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams and Northern Ireland nationalist politician John Hume to end the crisis.

"I think all the indications are here in Ireland that as a result of the refusal of the British government to accept the proposals which were put to them by both Gerry Adams and John Hume last week, that it now appears virtually non-existent, the prospect of a renewal of the IRA cessation," he said in an interview with CNN News.
The IRA ended its 17-month truce in February with a bomb attack in London. Since then the IRA has staged further attacks in Germany and Northern Ireland.

Major rejected suggestions by Adams and Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) and a key peace negotiator, that Sinn Fein be granted immediate inclusion in the peace talks if the IRA called a truce.
Major, who must call a general election by next May, said on Sunday that he would not accept a "phoney" IRA truce just so their political wing could gain admission to the talks.

With an election so near and after losing his one-seat parliamentary majority on Friday after a Conservative member of parliament, angered over the closure of a local hospital, said he would not longer support the government, Major is even more dependent now on the support of nine Ulster Unionist legislators who want the province to stay British.

But with the peace talks seemingly deadlocked, security forces fear it could lead to more IRA attacks or that the pro-British loyalist guerrillas could be lured back into the conflict after their two-year ceasefire.
After talks in London on Monday Major and his Irish counterpart John Bruton urged the IRA to renew the truce but even they could not agree on the timetable for bringing Sinn Fein into the talks.
Major insisted that he had never been prepared to put a date on it but Bruton told reporters that if a Christmas ceasefire was called he hoped it would be possible early in the New Year.
